transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Thank you for calling S-Net customer service, my name is Marcus. How can I help you today?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Hello Marcus. I'm having a really annoying problem with my broadband. Every time we get heavy rain, the whole connection just drops completely.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: I can certainly look into that line dropping issue for you today. May I start with your full name and account number, please?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes, it's Aaliyah Rahman, and my account number is SN 849 2011.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Thank you, Aaliyah. For account security, could you please confirm your full billing address and your memorable security question answer?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Sure, it's 14 Meadowbank Grove, Leeds, LS16 8PX. And the answer to the security question is Bluebell.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That's verified your account, thank you. Now, you mentioned the connection cuts out whenever there is heavy rainfall?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes, exactly. It's been happening for two weeks now. Yesterday during the downpour it went off four times, and I lost two critical work video calls. It is extremely disruptive.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Losing connection during important work calls is really stressful, Aaliyah, and I'm very sorry you've had to deal with that disruption.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Thank you Marcus, I appreciate that. I just need it to be stable.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: So to make sure I understand the situation clearly: your internet connection drops out intermittently specifically during wet weather, while staying mostly fine when dry, is that right?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes, that is spot on. When it's dry it works, but the moment rain starts it drops sync.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Understood. When the connection drops, what do the lights on the front of your S-Net router look like?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: The internet light, which is normally solid white, starts flashing orange, and then it goes solid red for about five minutes before it turns white again.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Okay, that indicates the router is losing the physical DSL sync signal from the street cabinet. Which model of hub do you have there?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: It's the black Hub 3 router that you sent when I signed up last autumn.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Got it, the Hub 3. And how is the Hub connected to your telephone wall socket? Is it using a plug-in microfilter or a filtered faceplate?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: It has a little white rectangular plastic box plugged into the master socket, with two cables coming out of it.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Right, that's a standard plug-in microfilter. Do you also have a landline telephone handset plugged into that same filter?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes, we have our cordless home phone base station plugged into the phone port on it.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Have you noticed any noise, crackling, or hissing sounds on the landline phone when you make or receive calls during rain?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Actually, yes! When my mother phoned me yesterday during the rainstorm, there was a terrible buzzing and crackling sound on the line.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That is very helpful diagnostic information. Audible crackling during rain strongly suggests moisture affecting the copper pair or a faulty filter.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Oh really? Could rainwater be getting into the cable outside our house?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: It is possible if there is a degraded junction box outside, or it could be internal damp affecting the microfilter. I am going to test the line now.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Okay, please go ahead.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Bear with me for a couple of minutes while I run our metallic line test and check the signal-to-noise ratio history on your circuit.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Thank you for your patience while that completed, Aaliyah. The line diagnostic test has returned its results.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: What does it show, Marcus? Did it find anything?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: The copper line test from the exchange to your master socket is showing a clear line with normal loop resistance and no battery fault or earth contact.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Wait, so the external cable is fine? Why does it drop when it rains then?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: However, the line error logs show a massive spike in errored seconds and high-frequency attenuation dropouts corresponding to high humidity periods.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: What does that mean in plain English?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Where is your telephone master socket located in the house? Is it near an external door, window, or hallway that gets damp?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: It is right by our front door in the porch, actually. The porch window tends to get a lot of condensation whenever it rains.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That explains a lot. If condensation gets into that small microfilter box, the tiny capacitor inside leaks high-frequency signal to earth.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Oh wow, I hadn't thought of that. Let me look at the microfilter right now.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Could you unplug the microfilter and inspect the little gold pins inside the socket where the broadband cable clips in?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Hold on... oh yes! Looking inside with my phone torch, there is a greenish-white crusty residue on two of the little pins.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That green crust is copper verdigris corrosion. When damp air hits that corroded contact, it shorts the high-frequency DSL frequencies.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That is exactly what must be happening! So the microfilter is ruined?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Yes, that microfilter is definitely degraded and causing your drops. Do you have a spare microfilter in the original S-Net box?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Let me check the cupboard under the stairs... Yes! I kept the welcome box with all the spare cables and there is a sealed spare filter here.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Brilliant. Let's unplug that corroded filter completely, plug the fresh new filter into the master socket, and reconnect the Hub and phone.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Okay, doing that right now. Old one out, new one plugged firmly into the master socket. Grey DSL cable clicked in, phone cable clicked in.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Excellent. Let's give the Hub 3 about thirty to forty seconds to renegotiate its handshake with the cabinet.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: The light is flashing green at the moment, and now it has gone solid white.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Just to check now that it has renegotiated, is the internet light remaining solid white without any orange flashing?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes, it is rock solid white, no flashing at all.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: I can see on my telemetry that the line has synced at 73.8 megabits per second, with a clean 6.2 decibel signal-to-noise ratio margin.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That is even faster than what we were getting before!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: The corroded filter was introducing severe line resistance. I have also reset the DLM dynamic line management profile so it clears the historical error count.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That's wonderful. Can I check if my laptop connects properly through the Wi-Fi now?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Please do. Try loading a few websites or streaming a quick video to make sure the data throughput is flowing smoothly.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Okay, opening my work portal and news website... wow, they loaded instantly. And BBC iPlayer started immediately without buffering.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Could you also pick up the home phone handset and check if the crackling noise is gone?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Listening to the dial tone now... it is completely silent in the background. The dial tone is crystal clear!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: So both your broadband connection and your telephone line are fully clear and running at top performance now, Aaliyah?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes, completely sorted. Everything is working perfectly now. Thank you so much Marcus!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: I am also placing an order for a spare heavy-duty filtered faceplate to be sent out in the post for you free of charge, to keep as a backup.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That is so thoughtful of you. I really appreciate the excellent help today.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: You are very welcome. Is there anything else at all I can help you with today?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: No, that's everything. You've solved it completely.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Thank you for choosing S-Net, Aaliyah. Have a wonderful rest of your day.
